How Tide Pools Work

By Ada Marsh

Twice a day the ocean pulls back from rocky shores and leaves behind tide pools: small basins of seawater that become, for a few hours, isolated worlds. The animals that live in them have to cope with heat, changing salinity and hungry birds until the water returns.

Zones of the shore

Ecologists divide the shore into zones by how long each one spends under water. The splash zone is wet only from spray, while the low intertidal zone is uncovered for just a short time at the lowest tides. Each zone hosts a different community.

  • Splash zone: lichens and periwinkles.
  • High intertidal: barnacles and limpets.
  • Low intertidal: sea stars, anemones and kelp.

Surviving low tide

Anemones close up to keep water in. Mussels clamp their shells shut. Some snails seal themselves to the rock with mucus. These behaviours buy time until the sea comes back, and they are the reason a tide pool can be so crowded with life.

A tide pool is a laboratory that resets itself twice a day.
